fields.meta_description: The sections an interview evaluation form needs, a 1-5 scale with written anchors, and an app that collects every interviewer's scores.
fields.h1: Build an Interview Evaluation Form That Scores Every Round
fields.hero_description: An interview evaluation form records how a candidate did against a role's criteria, on one shared scale. Emergent builds the form and a table of every panelist's scores.
fields.features_subheading: Most top-ranking interview evaluation forms are one-page PDFs. Emergent keeps the sections and adds sealed scores.
fields.feature_1:
A header that names the round

Records the candidate, the role, the round and the interviewer on every scorecard, with today's date filled in. A phone screen and a final panel stay separate entries for one person.
fields.feature_2:
Five levels, each with an anchor

Defines every point on the 1-5 scale in words the panel agrees on before the first interview. A 2 on communication then means the same thing whichever interviewer wrote it down.
fields.feature_3:
Criteria written for the job

Lists the handful of skills the role depends on, each paired with the question that tests it. A support lead is scored on calming an angry caller; a controller on closing the month.
fields.feature_4:
An evidence line under each score

Requires a sentence on what the candidate said or did before any score saves. "Walked through the vendor dispute step by step" holds up in a debrief. "Seemed sharp" does not.
fields.feature_5:
One recommendation, one reason

Closes with four choices, strong hire, hire, no hire and strong no hire, plus the main reason in a sentence. With no neutral middle, every interviewer has to take a side.
fields.feature_6:
Source code in your GitHub

Exports the whole app and its database to your GitHub repository. Your engineers can host it themselves or connect it to the applicant tracking system your recruiters use.
fields.why_description: Every interviewer's scores land in a database table your company owns, with no cap on responses and the full source ready to export.

fields.usecase_heading: Scorecards for Four Kinds of Interview
fields.tab_content_1:
Nobody reads a scorecard until all four are in

Panel scores bend toward whoever speaks first. At Northwind Logistics, four panelists interview an operations manager candidate, and no one sees another's scorecard until all four have submitted. With 3 of 4 in, hiring manager Dana Whitfield sees who is still writing. The debrief opens with every score side by side.
fields.tab_content_2:
Problem solving counts double in each candidate's score

Engineering rounds rarely weigh every skill the same. In a backend live-coding round, code quality and communication count once each, and the form says why. Interviewers rate each skill out of 5 and the app works out a weighted score. Anyone at 3.5 or higher moves to the onsite.
fields.tab_content_3:
When two faculty totals split by 5, a third reads

Admissions interviews run in long days. A radiography program has two faculty members score every applicant out of 25. When their totals sit 5 or more points apart, the app assigns a third faculty member before that applicant is ranked. The program director ranks the class from the settled totals.
fields.tab_content_4:
The student leaves with two things to practice

Students come to a mock interview for the notes. A career center evaluator rates six criteria at the end of each session. Within the hour, the student gets every score on their phone, with the two lowest criteria named as the work to do before booking the next mock.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Interview Evaluation Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps for whoever runs the hiring loop. Settle what you measure and how you score it before anyone meets a candidate.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the criteria the job depends on
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Anchor every point on the scale
fields.howto_step_1_des: Ask the people who do the work which skills separate a strong hire from a weak one, and keep four to six. Leave out anything you cannot tie to a task in the job description, like hobbies or where someone grew up.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the question that tests each criterion and ask it of every candidate in the same order. The US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) calls this a structured interview: the same job-related questions, scored the same way. A follow-up question is fine; a new topic is not.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Describe what a 1, a 3 and a 5 sound like for each criterion. OPM guidance puts rating scales at 3 to 7 levels, with at least three of them labeled. Written examples at each level keep one interviewer's 4 comparable with another's.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Score each criterion equally unless you can write down why one matters more. OPM recommends equal weights by default and a documented reason for anything else. Put that reason on the form itself, where every panelist reads it before scoring.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Ask each interviewer to submit within a day and before any discussion, and keep each panelist's scores hidden from the rest until everyone is done. Then meet, start with the criteria where ratings differ most, and agree a final rating.
fields.howto_step_6_des: End the form with a hire decision and the reason behind it. Leaving out a neutral option forces a position. The reason should point back to evidence written under the scores, not to a general impression of the person.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Store each scorecard with the candidate's record, including candidates you did not hire. Federal rules require employers to keep records having to do with hiring for one year. Ask counsel whether a longer period applies in your state.

plan.angle: Nine of the top ten are blank one-page PDFs and Word files from HR offices (Wisconsin, Case Western, Clemson, Mass.gov, SHRM, LinkedIn) plus one glossary page. They all carry the same parts: a header, a 1-5 scale, job-related criteria, comments and a hire recommendation. This page gives that form section by section, with anchored scale levels and an evidence line per score, then builds what paper cannot: scores hidden from other panelists until everyone submits, weighted rubrics that compute themselves, a third reader when two scorers split, and feedback sent to the candidate.
tab_stories: Four panelists interview a candidate for an operations manager role at Northwind Logistics; each one's scorecard stays hidden from the others until all four have submitted, and with three in, the hiring manager waits on the last before the debrief opens.

A backend engineering live-coding round counts problem solving twice and code quality and communication once each; the weighted score is computed per candidate and anyone at 3.5 or higher moves to the onsite.

A radiography program interviews applicants for its next class; two faculty score each applicant out of 25, and when their totals are 5 or more points apart a third faculty member scores the applicant before ranking.

A college career center runs mock interviews; the evaluator scores six criteria and the student gets a feedback email on their phone naming the two lowest-scored criteria as the things to practice before the next session.
